extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, advanced students, and participants in the International Congress of Mathematicians
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, formulating, and solving significant mathematical problems and for establishing rigorous foundations (axioms, existence, compatibility). Covers desiderata for problems, standards for proofs, methodological advice (generalization/specialization), and pointers to important open problems and methods (e.g., calculus of variations, functional equations, groups, axioms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and ease of comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical problem (and theory) should be so clear and easily comprehended that it attracts interest; what is clear attracts, the complicated repels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert quotes an old French mathematician: 'A mathematical theory is not to be considered complete until you have made it so clear that you can explain it to the first man whom you meet on the street.' He insists this clearness is even more desirable for a perfect mathematical problem. Clear, easily comprehended problems attract investigators and stimulate productive work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate difficulty (enticing but accessible)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical problem should be difficult in order to entice us, yet not completely inaccessible, lest it mock our efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems should serve as guide posts toward hidden truths and provide pleasure in successful solutions. Examples: Bernoulli's brachistochrone sparked calculus of variations; Fermat's problem led to deep developments in number theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance/usefulness of the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem's deep significance for the advance of mathematical science determines its enduring value; good problems often yield new methods and outlooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert cites Fermat's Last Theorem and the three-body problem as examples where specific questions produced broad theories (ideal numbers, celestial mechanics methods). Problems that interconnect branches (shortest line problem, regular polyhedra) are particularly valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite, exact hypotheses and finite-step proofs (rigor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect solution must be established by a finite number of steps based upon a finite number of hypotheses which are implied in the statement of the problem and which must always be exactly formulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the requirement of rigor: exact formulation of hypotheses and finite logical deduction. Hilbert emphasizes that rigor is necessary for exactness of results and for the problem to have its full effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor promotes simplicity and generality
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigor in proof is not enemy of simplicity; pursuit of rigor often leads to simpler, more general methods and to developments unavailable to less rigorous approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert gives examples: function-theoretical methods simplified algebraic curve theory; Weierstrass' work simplified calculus of variations foundations. Seeking rigor often forces discovery of simpler proofs and more developable methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact axiomatization for new concepts and signs
rubrics_metrics.description: When new mathematical concepts (especially geometric or physical) are introduced, they must be investigated axiomatically so that their exactness and deductive applicability match arithmetical concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New signs and geometric figures are mnemonic but their use as rigorous proof presupposes mastery of underlying axioms. Geometrical signs should be incorporated into the mathematical corpus only after rigorous axiomatic investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose notational/sign conventions to reflect phenomena but ground them in axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: New symbols should be chosen to remind us of the phenomena prompting the concepts, yet their correct use is determined by axioms underlying those concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: geometric figures as mnemonic of space intuition; arithmetical symbols as written diagrams. The analogy between arithmetic and geometry (use of pictures or intuition) is permissible only when axioms governing their use are clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek a more general standpoint / general methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure often arises from not recognizing the more general standpoint from which a problem is a single link; finding that standpoint yields methods applicable to related problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert cites Cauchy's complex integration paths and Kummer's ideals as instances where introducing a broader viewpoint produced powerful general methods. Finding general methods is often the most practicable and certain route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization and reduction to simpler problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialization—finding and solving simpler, related problems—is a principal lever to overcome difficulties and often a necessary step toward the main problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert argues that unsolved problems frequently fail because easier sub-problems were not solved; solving these simpler items with perfect devices and generalizable concepts often enables the original problem's solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove impossibility when solution is unattainable under given hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: When a solution cannot be achieved under the given hypotheses or in the intended sense, one should aim to prove the impossibility of such a solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical role: ancients proving impossibility (e.g., irrational ratio in isosceles right triangle). Later proofs of impossibility (e.g., impossibility of certain classical constructions) have provided satisfactory and rigorous settlements of questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical existence via non-contradiction (consistency implies existence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If assigned attributes do not lead to contradiction by a finite number of logical processes, then the mathematical existence of the concept is thereby proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert frames the proof of compatibility (consistency) of axioms as simultaneously proving the mathematical existence of structures (e.g., the continuum). A contradictory set of attributes means the concept does not exist mathematically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility/consistency of axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: An important requirement for foundations is to prove that the chosen axioms are not contradictory (i.e., cannot lead to a contradiction by a finite number of logical steps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert describes methods: model constructions (fields) to show geometric axioms depend on arithmetic consistency, and calls for direct proofs of arithmetic axioms' compatibility (introducing Archimedes and completeness axioms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolate dependent axioms to obtain independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate whether single axioms depend upon others and isolate parts in common so as to arrive at a system of axioms independent of one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert highlights the desire for a set of axioms containing exact and complete descriptions of relations among elementary ideas, and stresses isolating dependencies as a key foundational task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model-building to test axioms (constructive consistency proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct suitable models (e.g., fields of numbers) in which axioms correspond to arithmetic relations; contradictions in axioms become visible in the model, so models can demonstrate compatibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In geometry, proving compatibility can be effected by constructing a field of numbers where geometric axioms correspond to arithmetic relations. Thus geometry's consistency depends on arithmetic's.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary strong regularity assumptions; derive regularity when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume differentiability or other strong regularity properties unless necessary; investigate whether such properties can be derived from weaker axioms or from the group/concept itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert questions Lie's assumption of differentiability in transformation groups and asks whether differentiability is a consequence of the group concept and other axioms; similarly suggests studying functional equations without assuming differentiability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate functional equations under minimal hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional and difference equations should be studied without imposing unnecessary differentiability; explore what assertions remain valid under weaker hypotheses and how existence/regularity can be deduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He notes Abel's functional equations and examples where only non-differentiable functions solve certain functional equations; calls for general study of functional equations beyond differentiable cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of general principles to prove existence theorems (extend Dirichlet’s principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to prove existence theorems (e.g., in boundary-value problems, minimal surfaces, curvature problems) via a general principle analogous to Dirichlet's principle, possibly extending it and relaxing conditions on boundary data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert suggests current methods (based on potential theory) are insufficient for more general existence problems; proposes a general principle to show many regular variational problems have solutions under suitable continuity/differentiability of boundary data or suitably extended notions of solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and extend Weierstrass and Jacobi conditions in calculus of variations
rubrics_metrics.description: For variational problems, use the vanishing of the first variation, Jacobi's condition and Weierstrass's expression E and investigate necessity and sufficiency of Jacobi+E>0 for minima; relate first-order PDEs and characteristics to ordinary Euler–Lagrange equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert outlines the relationship between the second-order Euler–Lagrange ODE and a first-order PDE for the 'p' function, Weierstrass's formula and E(y') to compare integrals, and indicates these methods extend to multiple integrals. He references Kneser's modern treatment and Weierstrass' foundational work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer definite, special problems as catalysts of development
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularly definite and special problems attract attention and often exert lasting influence on the development of science; such problems commonly produce fundamental methods and theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert uses historical examples (brachistochrone, Fermat, three-body problem) to show specific, concrete problems can spawn entire theories (calculus of variations, ideal numbers, Poincaré's contributions). He therefore favors posing clear, definite problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain unity of mathematics through invention of sharper tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Advances should go hand in hand with invention of sharper tools and simpler methods that assist understanding earlier theories and reduce fragmentation of branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert argues that despite growth and specialization, mathematics remains an indivisible whole; the development of broadly useful methods enables individuals to work across areas more easily than in other sciences.
